items.followUp: Write the reactions of chlorine and bromine with water.

rubric.why: Checks the reaction of fluorine with water.
rubric.description: Correctly writes fluorine’s reaction with water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correctly balanced equation.

rubric.why: Checks that another halogen forms a hydrogen halide and a hypohalous acid with water.
rubric.description: Correctly writes the reaction of chlorine, bromine, or iodine with water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct equation; reversible arrows are acceptable.

modelAnswer: Fluorine reacts vigorously with water: 2F₂ + 2H₂O → 4HF + O₂.
Chlorine reacts reversibly with water: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO.
Bromine reacts reversibly with water: Br₂ + H₂O ⇌ HBr + HBrO.
Iodine reacts only slightly with water: I₂ + H₂O ⇌ HI + HIO.

items.followUp: State any four postulates of Bohr’s atomic theory.

rubric.why: Checks the arrangement and permitted paths of electrons in the atom.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed shells or circular orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the central nucleus and 1 mark for fixed electron paths or shells.

rubric.why: Checks that each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
rubric.description: States that each orbit or shell has a fixed energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixed-energy postulate.

rubric.why: Checks why electrons in permitted orbits do not lose energy continuously.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not radiate energy while remaining in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the no-radiation postulate.

rubric.why: Checks how an electron changes between energy levels.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs or emits energy when it jumps between orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the transition and energy-change postulate.

modelAnswer: An atom has a small, positively charged nucleus at its centre, and electrons revolve around it.
Electrons can revolve only in certain permitted circular orbits, called shells or energy levels.
Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
An electron in a permitted orbit does not radiate or lose energy.
An electron absorbs or emits energy when it moves between energy levels; the energy change is ΔE = hν.

items.followUp: Classify mixtures into homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of a mixture and that its components are not chemically combined.
rubric.description: Defines a mixture as two or more substances physically combined, with each retaining its properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two or more substances and 1 mark for physical combination or retention of properties.

rubric.why: Checks the homogeneous class and a suitable example.
rubric.description: Identifies a homogeneous mixture as uniform throughout and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the classification and example.

rubric.why: Checks the heterogeneous class and a suitable example.
rubric.description: Identifies a heterogeneous mixture as non-uniform and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the classification and example.

modelAnswer: A mixture is a physical combination of two or more substances in any proportion; its components retain their properties and can be separated by physical methods.
A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout; examples include salt water and air.
A heterogeneous mixture does not have a uniform composition throughout; examples include oil and water or sand and water.

items.followUp: Define metallic bonding and draw a labelled diagram showing the arrangement of particles in a metal.

rubric.why: Checks the definition and the particles involved in metallic bonding.
rubric.description: Defines a metallic bond as the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying positive ions and electrons, and 1 mark for the electrostatic attraction between them.

rubric.why: Checks the arrangement of the metal ions.
rubric.description: Explains that positive metal ions are arranged in a regular lattice.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the regular lattice of positive ions.

rubric.why: Checks that the electrons are free to move through the structure.
rubric.description: Explains that delocalised electrons move throughout the lattice.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the mobile or delocalised electrons.

rubric.why: Checks that the diagram represents and labels both parts of the metallic structure.
rubric.description: Provides a labelled diagram showing positive ions surrounded by mobile electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear, correctly labelled diagram.

modelAnswer: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons surrounding them.
The metal atoms release their outer electrons, which become delocalised and move throughout the structure.
The positive ions remain arranged in a regular lattice, and the attraction between them and the mobile electrons holds the metal together.
Diagram:
M⁺       M⁺       M⁺   ← positive metal ions
e⁻  e⁻  e⁻  e⁻      ← delocalised, mobile electrons
M⁺       M⁺       M⁺   ← positive metal ions

items.followUp: Define vapour pressure and explain how temperature and intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Checks the definition under equilibrium conditions.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure as the pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for pressure due to vapour and equilibrium with the liquid.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of temperature.
rubric.description: Explains that vapour pressure increases as temperature increases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship.

rubric.why: Checks how the liquid’s nature and intermolecular forces affect evaporation.
rubric.description: Explains that weaker intermolecular forces give a higher vapour pressure, while stronger forces give a lower one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between intermolecular forces and vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of adding a non-volatile dissolved substance.
rubric.description: States that a non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of a liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container at a given temperature.
As temperature increases, more liquid molecules escape into the vapour phase, so vapour pressure increases.
The nature of the liquid affects its vapour pressure: weaker intermolecular forces give a higher vapour pressure, while stronger forces give a lower vapour pressure.
A dissolved non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the liquid.

items.followUp: Define a diatomic molecule and give two examples other than nitrogen and oxygen.

rubric.why: Checks the defining number of atoms in a diatomic molecule.
rubric.description: Defines a diatomic molecule as a molecule containing two atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it contains two atoms.

rubric.why: Checks that suitable examples are given.
rubric.description: Gives two correct examples of diatomic molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correct examples.

modelAnswer: A diatomic molecule is a molecule made up of two atoms.
Examples include H₂ and O₂.

items.followUp: State two differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: Checks the composition of an element.
rubric.description: States that an element contains only one kind of atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct description of an element.

rubric.why: Checks the composition and chemical combination in a compound.
rubric.description: States that a compound contains two or more different elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct description of a compound.

modelAnswer: An element is a pure substance made up of only one kind of atom.
A compound is a pure substance made up of two or more different elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion.

items.followUp: Write the electronic configurations of carbon and fluorine.

rubric.why: Checks nitrogen’s shell configuration.
rubric.description: Gives nitrogen’s electronic configuration as 2,5.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct configuration.

rubric.why: Checks oxygen’s shell configuration.
rubric.description: Gives oxygen’s electronic configuration as 2,6.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct configuration.

modelAnswer: Nitrogen has atomic number 7; its electronic configuration is 2,5.
Oxygen has atomic number 8; its electronic configuration is 2,6.
